Discover Association Rules from Sequential or Transaction Data

Source: R/association_rules.R
association_rules.Rd

association_rules() finds association rules of the form {A} -> {B} with the Apriori algorithm (Agrawal & Srikant, 1994): sets of items that occur together in at least min_support of the transactions, and the rules among them that pass min_confidence and min_lift. It reads a list of transactions, a wide data frame or matrix of states, a 0/1 incidence table, or a network: the sequences behind a netobject or tna model become transactions of their distinct states, and a one-hot network's windows become transactions of their active codes.

Support is how common the whole rule is, confidence how often B occurs when A does, and lift how much more often A and B occur together than they would if they were independent (see Metrics). A sequence read as a transaction loses its order, so a rule says that states occur in the same sequence, not that one follows the other; build_network() models order. The rules are not tested for significance, and lowering the thresholds quickly multiplies them, so check whether a rule of interest stays when min_support changes.

Usage

association_rules(
  x,
  min_support = 0.1,
  min_confidence = 0.5,
  min_lift = 1,
  max_length = 5L,
  format = c("auto", "binary")
)

# S3 method for class 'net_association_rules'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_association_rules'
summary(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_association_rules'
plot(x, ...)

Arguments

x

The transactions, in one of these forms:

netobject

Each sequence in its data becomes a transaction of its distinct states. In a one-hot network the codes are the items and each window is one transaction. A network without data, and an association network (cor, pcor, glasso, ising, mgm), whose rows are variables, raise an error; a netobject_group raises one of class nestimate_bad_input (pass one group's network). A bare cograph_network is read as a netobject, a tna model by its sequence data, and an mcml by its between-cluster network, so its items are the clusters.

list

A plain list holding one character vector of items per transaction.

data frame

Each row is a transaction of its distinct non-missing states. The frame must be a single column or a numbered run of position columns (T1, T2, ...) with nothing beside it; otherwise it raises an error of class nestimate_bad_input; declare the columns with build_network(state_cols = ) and pass the network instead. A column called action and repeated column names are refused the same way. A frame of 0/1 or logical columns is a binary table, one column per item, read with format = "binary".

matrix

A character matrix is read like a character data frame. A numeric or logical matrix is a binary transaction table (rows are transactions, columns are items, named I1, I2, ... when the matrix has no column names).

Binary input must hold only 0/1 or TRUE/FALSE: a missing cell or any other value raises an error of class nestimate_bad_input. For the print() and plot() methods: a net_association_rules object.

min_support

The smallest share of transactions an itemset must occur in to be frequent, above 0 and at most 1. Default 0.1. It is applied as a count, ceiling(min_support * n_transactions).

min_confidence

The smallest confidence a rule must have, between 0 and 1. Default 0.5.

min_lift

The smallest lift a rule must have, at least 0. Default 1, which keeps rules whose items occur together at least as often as independence predicts.

max_length

The largest itemset size searched, at least 2. Default 5.

format

How 0/1 columns are read. Columns of only 0 and 1 could be items or recoded positions, so with "auto" (default) they raise an error of class nestimate_bad_input. "binary" declares them items, one row per transaction; it raises the same error on a data frame with any other value.

...

For the print(), summary() and plot() methods: ignored.

object

For the summary() method: a net_association_rules object.

Value

A net_association_rules object. print() shows the counts, the thresholds and the ten rules with the highest lift; summary() returns the rules table, one row per rule; plot() draws the rules by support and confidence. The object's fields:

rules

Data frame, one row per rule, ordered by decreasing lift and then confidence, with columns antecedent and consequent (the itemsets as comma-separated strings), support, confidence, lift, conviction, count (transactions holding the whole rule) and n_transactions.

frequent

Data frame, one row per frequent itemset, with columns itemset, size, support and count.

frequent_itemsets

List of the frequent itemsets per size k, each entry a list of items, count and support.

items

Character vector of the frequent single items the mining ran on (all items when none reaches min_support).

n_transactions

Number of transactions.

n_rules

Number of rules.

params

List of min_support, min_confidence, min_lift and max_length.

The print() method returns its input invisibly. summary() returns the rules data frame described above. plot() prints a scatter plot of support against confidence, with point size and colour showing lift, and returns the ggplot object invisibly; with no rules it says so in a message and returns NULL invisibly.

Details

Algorithm

Level-wise Apriori (Agrawal & Srikant, 1994) with the full pruning step: after the join step generates the candidates of size k, every subset of size k - 1 is checked to be frequent before support is counted, which keeps the search fast at k >= 4. Support of pairs is counted with crossprod(), of larger itemsets by logical indexing. Every split of a frequent itemset into a non-empty antecedent and consequent is a candidate rule.

Metrics

support

P(A and B): the share of transactions holding both the antecedent and the consequent.

confidence

P(B | A): the share of transactions holding the antecedent that also hold the consequent.

lift

P(A and B) / (P(A) P(B)). Values above 1 indicate positive association, below 1 negative association.

conviction

(1 - P(B)) / (1 - confidence), the departure from independence in the direction of the rule (Brin et al., 1997); higher means a stronger implication, and a rule with confidence 1 has conviction Inf.

References

Agrawal, R. & Srikant, R. (1994). Fast algorithms for mining association rules. In Proc. 20th VLDB Conference, 487–499.

Brin, S., Motwani, R., Ullman, J. D. & Tsur, S. (1997). Dynamic itemset counting and implication rules for market basket data. In Proc. ACM SIGMOD, 255–264. (lift and conviction)

See also

build_network, predict_links

Examples

# From a list of transactions
trans <- list(
  c("plan", "discuss", "execute"),
  c("plan", "research", "analyze"),
  c("discuss", "execute", "reflect"),
  c("plan", "discuss", "execute", "reflect"),
  c("research", "analyze", "reflect")
)
rules <- association_rules(trans, min_support = 0.3, min_confidence = 0.5)
print(rules)
#> Association Rules  [24 rules | 6 items | 5 transactions]
#>   Support >= 0.30  |  Confidence >= 0.50  |  Lift >= 1.00
#> 
#>   Top rules (by lift):
#>     1. analyze -> research  (sup=0.400 conf=1.000 lift=2.50)
#>     2. research -> analyze  (sup=0.400 conf=1.000 lift=2.50)
#>     3. discuss -> execute  (sup=0.600 conf=1.000 lift=1.67)
#>     4. execute -> discuss  (sup=0.600 conf=1.000 lift=1.67)
#>     5. discuss, plan -> execute  (sup=0.400 conf=1.000 lift=1.67)
#>     6. execute, plan -> discuss  (sup=0.400 conf=1.000 lift=1.67)
#>     7. discuss, reflect -> execute  (sup=0.400 conf=1.000 lift=1.67)
#>     8. execute, reflect -> discuss  (sup=0.400 conf=1.000 lift=1.67)
#>     9. discuss -> execute, plan  (sup=0.400 conf=0.667 lift=1.67)
#>     10. execute -> discuss, plan  (sup=0.400 conf=0.667 lift=1.67)
#>     ... and 14 more rules

# From a netobject (sequences as transactions)
seqs <- data.frame(
  V1 = sample(LETTERS[1:5], 50, TRUE),
  V2 = sample(LETTERS[1:5], 50, TRUE),
  V3 = sample(LETTERS[1:5], 50, TRUE)
)
net <- build_network(seqs, method = "relative")
rules <- association_rules(net, min_support = 0.1)
